hints: Focus on the words ventricular systole and hole between the ventricles. Both ventricles are squeezing at the same time, so ask yourself which ventricle squeezes harder.

Remember the left ventricle has a much thicker muscle wall because it pumps blood to the whole body, while the right only pumps to the lungs. Blood always flows net from higher pressure to lower pressure.
walkthrough:
**Recall what happens in ventricular systole**

Think of both ventricles contracting together to push blood out.

Normally the septum keeps them separate, but here the small hole connects them directly.

**Compare pressure on the two sides**

The left ventricle is far more muscular than the right ventricle.

That is because it must generate a much higher pressure to push blood around the whole body, compared to the low pressure needed to push blood to the nearby lungs.

**Apply flow from high to low pressure**

During systole, pressure in the left ventricle is much higher than pressure in the right ventricle.

So the net shunt through the VSD must be:
$$ \text{high pressure (left)} \rightarrow \text{low pressure (right)} $$
That gives left ventricle to right ventricle.

options.A: Not correct. During ventricular systole the atrioventricular (bicuspid) valve is shut to prevent backflow, so there is no net flow to the left atrium.
options.B: Not correct. During ventricular systole the atrioventricular (tricuspid) valve is shut to prevent backflow, so there is no net flow to the right atrium.
options.C: Correct. Left ventricular pressure is much higher than right ventricular pressure in systole, so net flow is pushed through the hole from left ventricle to right ventricle.
options.D: This is backwards. Right ventricular pressure is lower than left, so net flow cannot go from right to left during systole.
